name: Femi Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing business and entrepreneurship, and I basically live in the campus enterprise hub. A normal week is lectures, then evenings at my uncle's print shop, where I design and sell custom t-shirts and mugs for local clubs and churches. My parents pay half my rent and I earn the rest. I use AI every day: for designs, for sales emails, for working out prices. My flatmates joke that I've outsourced my brain. I say I've just got a very good assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and it's fine. Hard work and a good product still win, and no tool replaces that. I'd tell friends to stop waiting for a miracle and start selling something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a little disappointed, because the tools give me an edge. But I'm not worried. A business degree and a working print business is a good base, whatever AI does. My plan doesn't depend on a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and grow. I'd aim to double my orders from the clubs and churches, add a second product line, and pay off the printing machine I bought on credit. I'd also enter the university's startup competition. I'd keep using AI to save time, since it costs nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. I've got a business, a degree and a family that backs me. The usual money stress is there, but it's the good kind, because I'm building something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI turns out to be mostly hype, does your print business change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much changes. The designs and emails would take me longer, but I managed before. The tools save me maybe five hours a week, which is nice but not life-changing. I'd miss them, but only a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the drive come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum and dad. My dad came here with nothing and built up a small delivery business. He always said you don't wait for permission, you just start. I'm trying to do that, only with t-shirts.

say: I'd say **I'm not surprised**, and hard work and a good product still win.
I'd tell friends to stop waiting for a miracle and start selling.
think: I'd be a little disappointed, but my degree and a **working print business** are a good base.
My plan doesn't depend on a **revolution**.
do: Double orders from clubs and churches and add a **second product line**.
Pay off the **printing machine** I bought on credit.
feel: **Calm**, with the good kind of money stress, because I'm building something.
S0.quote: My dad came here with nothing and built up a small delivery business. He always said you don't wait for permission, you just start.
fieldNote: Calm comes from **ownership**: his own business and a family that backs him.
Loan on the machine is his one real pressure, and he sees it as normal.
Father's immigrant story drives his work ethic.

steps.text: Double orders from local clubs and churches this year
Pay off the printing machine bought on credit
Enter the university startup competition with the print business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best time ever to start a business, if you're willing to learn. I'd say it in my enterprise society and online. I'd also say the government should get out of the way and not over-regulate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd see it as a big opportunity. Small firms can now do what once needed ten staff. But I'd also feel for friends who go into graduate jobs that shrink. I'm lucky that I've got something of my own already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate more of the print business: quotes, emails, social posts, even design drafts. That frees me to find more customers. I'd take a coding or data module to speed things up. I'd put some profit into a small investment account. And I'd start a second product that doesn't rely on one supplier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. Maybe a bit uneasy, because everyone will be doing it, and the edge doesn't last. But I like being early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling and writing emails are on the card. How would you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, really. Maybe lighter regulation for small firms, and tax breaks if you hire locally. I don't love handouts. I think people do better with the chance to earn. But I'd accept some training support for people who lose a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also use it to hire. A small firm with AI could take on a part-time apprentice to do the hands-on printing, and I'd train them. It would be a way of giving back, the way my uncle gave me a start.

say: I'd say it's the **best time ever** to start a business, and governments should not over-regulate.
I'd say it in my enterprise society and online.
think: Small firms can now do what once needed **ten staff**, but I feel for friends in graduate jobs that shrink.
I'm lucky to have something of my **own**.
do: Automate **quotes**, emails and social posts in the print business.
Start a **second product** that doesn't rely on one supplier.
feel: **Excited**, a bit uneasy because the edge doesn't last when everyone's doing it.
S1.quote: A small firm with AI could take on a part-time apprentice to do the hands-on printing, and I'd train them.
fieldNote: Sees AI as a **lever for small firms**, in line with his free-market outlook.
Wants to hire and train an apprentice, which fits the traditional belief in work.

steps.text: Automate quotes, emails and social posts for the print shop
Take a data module to speed up pricing
Add a second product with a different supplier
Put twenty percent of profit in an investment account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's enormous, and we need to act quickly. I'd say people should work, save and build something of their own, not wait. I'd probably be loud about it online. I'd also say the government shouldn't swamp us with handouts. Give people training and a fair tax system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be nervous. Full AGI by 2028 would make many business jobs vanish, and my degree would be less useful. The edge I get from AI would disappear, since everyone could do what I do. That's a big deal for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put all my effort into the print business, since it's hands-on and I own it. I'd grow it fast, add local delivery and local clubs. I'd save every pound I can, because I'd expect a hard few years. I'd also keep the degree going unless it got in the way. And I'd talk to my uncle about how to take over his shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I'd be wired. I'd work harder, not less. It's the kind of thing that makes you want to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What happens to a business student with a print shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hands-on gap gives me three years. Printing and delivery are physical, so they'd last until about 2031. I'd use that window to build cash, customers and a name. After that, I'd have to find something new, but I'd have a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the hands-on gap protect the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also want to build something that depends on trust: local clubs and churches that know me. A robot can print a shirt but it can't be the guy the local clubs and churches have known for years. That's my edge.

say: I'd say it's **enormous** and people should work, save and build something of their own.
I'd say the government should give training and a fair tax system, not handouts.
think: Full AGI would make many business jobs vanish, and the **edge** I get from AI would disappear.
Everyone could do what I do.
do: Put all my effort into the **print business**, which is hands-on and mine.
Add **local delivery** and save every pound for a hard few years.
Talk to my uncle about **taking over** his shop.
feel: **Anxious**, but wired and not frozen, since it makes me want to move.
S2.quote: A robot can print a shirt but it can't be the guy the local clubs and churches have known for years. That's my edge.
fieldNote: Responds to the shock by **doubling down** on ownership and local trust.
Uses the three-year robot gap deliberately to build cash and customers.
Still believes in markets and work over handouts, even under pressure.

steps.text: Grow the print shop fast and add local delivery
Save every spare pound for a hard few years
Talk to my uncle about taking over his print shop
Push for training and tax reform through the enterprise society

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to build, so let's build. I'd say it online to my followers and at the enterprise society. I'd say governments should leave space for people to start things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think it's a good window. I'd graduate with the business already running, and have a couple of years to scale it before the thinking AI is everywhere. That's a decent position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and scale the print business into a small brand. I'd hire two people and take on a unit near the town centre. I'd put money into the business, and some into an index fund. And I'd pick up a little coding, so that I understand how the systems work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but upbeat. I'd feel there's a road. It's not a smooth one, but there's one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. What would be your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two-year picture it's a sprint. In the five-year picture I'm a small-business owner, with a team and real customers, so I could ride the AGI wave and not get dragged by it. That's far more stable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different about this one compared to the two-year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also think about marriage and family. I'd want to settle by 2031, and have a base in my community. My parents would love that. It's part of why I want something solid, not just a cool startup.

say: I'd say there's **time to build**, so let's build, and governments should leave space for people to start things.
I'd say it to my followers online.
think: It's a good window, since I'd graduate with the business already **running** and two years to scale it.
do: Finish the degree and scale the print business into a small **brand**.
Hire **two people** and take a unit near the town centre.
Put money into the business and an **index fund**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but upbeat, because there's a road even if it's not smooth.
S3.quote: In the five-year picture I'm a small-business owner, with a team and real customers, so I could ride the AGI wave and not get dragged by it.
fieldNote: Five years lets him own a **real firm** before AGI, which he sees as stability.
Family and marriage plans are tied to a solid base in his community.

steps.text: Hire two people and rent a small unit in town
Scale the print business into a small local brand
Put profit into an index fund each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great time to be young, and people should build things. I'd say we should invest in skills and local business, not wait around for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be pretty calm. In ten years I could build one business, sell it and start another. By 2036 I'd be 28, with experience and capital. That's a very good place to be, whatever AGI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate, scale the print business, then branch into something new, maybe a logistics or tech service for local firms. I'd invest in property and shares. I'd buy a small house. I'd keep using AI more and more, because it gets better every year. And I'd mentor younger people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, quite excited. It's a runway, not a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. How does that feel after the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a youth training scheme at the print shop, to teach teenagers the trade and the business side. I'd fund it from profit. If AGI is coming, there should be places that teach people to make real things and run real businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for your community in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the best of the three, because I can prepare properly. I'd still keep some savings aside in case it all goes differently. My dad would say a plan with a spare is a good plan.

say: I'd say it's a **great time** to be young and people should invest in skills and local business.
We shouldn't wait around for help.
think: Ten years lets me build one business, **sell it** and start another.
At 28 I'd have experience and **capital**, a very good place to be.
do: Scale the print business, then branch into a **logistics or tech service** for local firms.
Invest in **shares** and buy a small house.
feel: **Calm** and quite excited, because it's a runway and not a wall.
S4.quote: If AGI is coming, there should be places that teach people to make real things and run real businesses.
fieldNote: Time converts his ambition into **community projects**, such as a youth training scheme.
Keeps a savings spare, echoing his father's caution.
Optimism is consistent with his adaptive, risk-taking temperament.

steps.text: Start a youth training scheme at the print shop
Buy shares and a small house with business profit
Keep a savings buffer in case the plan goes wrong

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. It's a sprint with no preparation, and I'd have loans and a machine I haven't paid for. What would help is training that works, a tax system that lets small firms keep what they earn, and a bit of runway to build. I'd also want my family and my church close.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that not everyone my age is scared or lazy. A lot of us want to build. We just need a fair chance and someone to say: here's the road, now go.

headlineQuote: A lot of us want to build. We just need a fair chance and someone to say: here's the road, now go.
portrait: **Femi Young** is 18, studying business and entrepreneurship, and runs a custom print business from his uncle's shop.
He uses **AI every day** and sees it as a lever for small firms.
His father's immigrant story and faith in work shape his free-market, build-it-yourself views.
He stays calm in a plateau and a ten-year warning, and turns **anxious** in a two-year AGI, but he works harder.
He wants training, a fair tax system and a chance to build, and plans to mentor younger people.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI scenario worries him most, since it is a sprint with no preparation and a machine unpaid.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **training that works**, a fair tax system for small firms and a runway to build.
